payout_quote: NY Attorney General complaint form: 'The Attorney General is not my private attorney, but represents the public in enforcing laws designed to protect the public from misleading or unlawful business practices.' Restitution reaches consumers through AG enforcement — e.g., the September 2026 $694M multistate settlement with Credit Acceptance Corporation, where 'consumers eligible for restitution will be notified by a claims administrator.' This recovers YOUR OWN money taken by a business — it never promises any payout.
timing: Complaint filing is immediate (online in most states). Mediation outcomes and multistate-settlement payouts are slow — settlements take years, and eligible consumers are notified by a claims administrator after the deal closes.
biggest_catch: Filing a complaint does NOT make the AG your lawyer — the office 'cannot represent you in court or provide you with legal or financial advice,' and filing 'does not mean that the Attorney General has initiated a lawsuit or proceeding on my behalf or that it will do so.' Most complaints end in mediation or become enforcement intelligence; direct restitution to you usually comes only via a multistate settlement that happens to cover your case.
eligibility: Any consumer in the state with a complaint about a business's misleading or unlawful practices. You are generally expected to try resolving with the business first. Knowingly false complaints can be a misdemeanor (e.g., NY Penal Law).
steps: Find your state AG's consumer-complaint page — NAUPA-style hub https://naag.org links every state; e.g., Indiana files at in.gov/attorneygeneral/consumer-protection-division/file-a-complaint/ or by mail/fax.
First attempt to resolve the issue directly with the business (most AG offices require this).

File the complaint online (or by printable form) with copies — never originals — of contracts, receipts, and correspondence; note the resolution you want (refund, product delivery, service performed).
The AG's office may forward your complaint to the business for mediation, or use it as evidence in an enforcement action.

Watch for multistate settlements in your state: if one covers you, the claims administrator notifies you directly and you file with them — e.g., the Sept 2026 $694M Credit Acceptance settlement across 40+ states.
catches: The AG is not your private attorney and filing creates no obligation for the office to act on your case.
No legal advice and no court representation — for that you need a private attorney or small-claims court.
Restitution is uncertain and slow; most value comes from rare multistate settlements, not individual complaints.
Your complaint (and documents) may be shared with the business you complained about and with other agencies.
False statements on a complaint form can be a criminal misdemeanor.
notes: Verified 2026-09-22/23: state AG consumer-complaint mechanisms are live in every state checked (Indiana online filing, North Dakota and New York official forms), NAAG documents state-AG enforcement authority, and the Sept 2026 $694M Credit Acceptance multistate settlement shows the restitution path is current. In-app, this route must be framed as complaint-driven recovery with the 'not your lawyer' warning up front — never as guaranteed money. No app — state websites/forms only.

c1.evidence: State attorneys general are real government offices; NAAG (naag.org) is their official association.

c2.evidence: Official state pages document the consumer-complaint filing process (online/printable forms, e.g., Indiana, North Dakota, New York) and multistate settlements with claims administrators (e.g., $694M Credit Acceptance, Sept 2026).

c3.evidence: Filing a consumer complaint is free; no fee appears in any official form or process.

c4.evidence: Official forms state plainly what filing does and does not do (no private representation, no guaranteed action); settlement announcements state that eligible consumers are notified by the claims administrator.

s1.note: Any in-state consumer with a business complaint; must attempt direct resolution first; false complaints punishable.

s2.note: Free; no fee in the official process.

s3.note: Immediate filing; slow and uncertain resolution — settlements take years.

s4.note: No weasel words — official forms are blunt that the AG is not your attorney.

s5.note: https://naag.org — the official state-AG association hub linking every state.

s6.note: Steps are concrete: find state page, try the business first, file with copies, watch for settlements.
